newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian cabinet likely to discuss airline link-up.
newsitem.headline: Indian cabinet likely to discuss airline link-up.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet was expected on Tuesday to discuss a controversial proposed tie-up between Tata group and Singapore Airlines Ltd which has split the government.

The Industry Ministry last week approved the $600 million plan by Tata Industries Ltd and SIA to set up a domestic airline. "The proposal has been sent to the cabinet," a senior Industry Ministry official told Reuters.

The Industry Ministry's recommendation flew in the face of strong opposition from Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim, who wants a new aviation policy that would ban foreign investment in domestic airlines.

Newspapers said the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs was expected on Tuesday to discuss the proposal, which for some foreign investors has become a litmus test of the centre-left government's commitment to economic reform.
The controversial Tata-SIA tie-up was cleared in December by the Foreign Investment Promotion Board and forwarded to Deve Gowda's cabinet.
The board is a panel of senior government officials attached to the Industry Ministry which can approve foreign investment up to six billion rupees ($170 million). Larger deals need cabinet approval.
SIA and Tata Industries submitted their proposal to launch the airline in February 1995. The Tatas planned to take a 60 percent stake, with SIA holding the rest.
Since then, the proposal has languished in the government, caught in a high-stakes battle over whether to permit foreign investment in the civil aviation sector.
Ibrahim, a close ally of Deve Gowda, has been joined by communist partners in the 13-party United Front coalition in opposing the joint venture, arguing it would harm state-owned Indian Airlines.
"This is indiscriminate opening up of the economy," said D. Raja, a Communist Party of India (CPI) leader and a member of United Front's policy-making steering committee.
"We have been saying that the opening up of our skies will not benefit our domestic aviation industry," he said.
The Hindu nationalist opposition Bharatiya Janata Party has also vehemently opposed the proposed tie-up.
The communists and defenders of domestic industry say the government should take measures to strengthen Indian Airlines, which operates domestic routes, and Air India, which flies internationally.
But analysts said investors, both domestic and foreign, were wary of committing funds to India in absence of a clear and transparent policy framework.
"Ambiguities in policy affect investment decisions," said Subra Subramanian, an analyst with H.G. (India) Securities.
"Without foreign investment it is difficult to modernise and have an efficient domestic aviation industry," a spokesman for a private domestic airline who asked not to be identified said.
Currently the government reviews foreign companies' proposals on a case-by-case basis.
If approved, a foreign firm can take up to a 40 percent stake in a domestic airline. Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways each have stakes in India's Jet Airways.
Ibrahim has said Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways should be made to sell off their stakes to domestic investors.
